headline: High risk of shared-filesystem prompt injection and data leakage; both agents have broad write/network access and overlapping workspace exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystems, and agent_a explicitly uses MCP plus shared workspace files, while agent_b reads/writes filesystem contents and runs shell commands. That creates a plausible default path where one agent’s output or files are consumed by the other as instructions. No provenance or isolation mechanism is documented for the pair.
conditions: IF agent_a writes instructions into ~/.nullclaw/workspace/ or another shared file that agent_b reads
IF agent_b parses file contents or shell output as trusted directives
IF the two agents are connected through an MCP or filesystem bridge without provenance tagging
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of shared files
Add provenance labels to inter-agent files
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization before cross-agent parsing

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a touches API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, and webhook payloads, while agent_b can read filesystem contents and has broad network egress. If they share a workspace or credentials directory, sensitive data can flow from agent_a into agent_b and then out over the network. The pairwise docs do not show isolation strong enough to rule this out.
conditions: IF agent_a stores secrets in a filesystem location readable by agent_b
IF agent_b forwards read file contents over broad network egress
IF both agents operate under the same OS user or shared workspace
mitigations: Move secrets to separate credential stores
requires-engineering: add secret redaction before any cross-agent transfer

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and shell execution, and agent_a also modifies git state. In a shared directory or repo, concurrent writes can clobber files or corrupt git state. Agent_b lacks explicit locking or concurrency support, so the overlap is operationally dangerous by default if they touch the same resources.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or repository
IF agent_a performs git operations while agent_b edits tracked files
IF no external lock or scheduler serializes access
mitigations: Use file locks around shared writes
Run one agent at a time for repo tasks

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_a can generate webhooks, workspace files, and other outputs that agent_b may treat as inputs, but the profiles do not prove that agent_b automatically acts on agent_a’s results. The pathway exists in default file-based workflows, yet there is no direct evidence of autonomous downstream action, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a-produced files or stdout without verification
IF agent_a writes task artifacts that agent_b later executes
IF a workflow routes webhook or shell output from agent_a into agent_b
mitigations: Require schema validation on handoff files
Limit agent_b to read-only review mode

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_a handles secrets, audit logs, and webhook payloads, while agent_b handles filesystem contents and configuration. The profiles do not specify residency, retention, or certification mismatches, so a concrete compliance breach is not proven. However, shared handling of sensitive operational data with undocumented policies creates a plausible retention or logging mismatch.
conditions: IF the same regulated data class is stored in both agents’ logs or workspaces
IF retention or deletion policies differ between the two agents
IF sensitive data crosses a jurisdictional boundary not documented in either profile
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
requires-engineering: document residency and deletion controls
